newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans want more information on Euro-consumer group.
newsitem.headline: Germans want more information on Euro-consumer group.

text.p: Germans need more information about the planned European single currency if the distrust visible in a trial of the euro in Berlin is to be reversed, Germany's leading consumer group said on Wednesday.

Although the 10-day euro trial which began on Friday was intended to soothe fears about monetary union, financial analyst Volker Pietsch of the Verbraucherzentrale consumer body said it would not convince Berliners to give up their beloved mark.

"Consumers are suffering from a dire lack of information and I don't think this Euro Week is going to change that," Pietch said, referring to the programme in which Berliners can shop at over 50 selected stores with special-issue euros.

Over sixty percent of Germans remain sceptical about the euro, Pietch said, and feel unwilling to trade the deutschemark, a symbol of post-war economic stability and prosperity, for what they fear might be a less stable currency.

"People are terrified when they think of the euro, they fear their money will simply be taken away if monetary union becomes a reality," Pietsch said. "The programme this week is not pointless, but it is not enough."
For about a week before the euro trial was officially launched on Friday, Germans have been able to exchange currency at a rate of two marks to one euro.

Retailers, banks and the European Commission have spent millions of marks on publicity, informational brochures and the special-issue coins in an effort to build curiosity and a bit of faith among consumers about the euro.
But Pietsch said, "People think you can advertise the euro like you advertise detergent, with quick spots and bits of information."
LandesBank Berlin manufactured 1.3 million special coins for use during the trial in denominations of 1.5 euros (three marks) 2.5 euros (five marks) and 10 euros (20 marks).
Organisers insist they are meeting the goals they set for the week.
"By our measure, the programme is going very well in Berlin," LandesBank Berlin spokeswoman Constanze Stempel said. "The high demand for euros shows that people are at least interested."
The bank said that as of the weekend, it had exchanged over 400,000 euros for marks at branch offices and outdoor euro stands throughout the city, Stempel said.

"I think we can call this a success so far," Sabine Bachmann, a spokeswoman for the European Commission's Berlin office said. "We have a lot of people visiting our information stands, and that was our aim."

But many shoppers on Berlin's Alexanderplatz, where several shops are participating in the euro trial, referred to the euros as "Monopoly money" and say they are only interested in the coins as collectors' items.

"They may be nice to give to the children, but as a worker and a consumer, I don't see the advantages (of the monetary union)," Cornelia Kranz, 43, a saleswoman in a perfume store which is accepting Euros during the programme, said.

If European economic and monetary union (EMU) moves forward as planned, citizens in participating countries will see their national currencies phased out between January and July 2002 and replaced with the euro.
